2026-07-08B10-0337/2026Objection pursuant to Rule 114(3): Trajectory to decrease the contribution of high indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels to renewable energy targets

Discussion transcript

Objection pursuant to Rule 114(3): Trajectory to decrease the contribution of high indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels to renewable energy targets

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

The first vote is on the objection pursuant to Rule 114(3): Trajectory to decrease the contribution of high indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels to renewable energy targets (see minutes, item 10.1).

Dubravka Šuica

Mr President, honourable Members, I would like to encourage honourable Members to support the Commission Delegated Act on indirect land-use change and to vote against the tabled objection.

In the latest review, it was found that both palm oil and soy beans qualify as feedstock with a high risk of indirect land-use change and therefore the Commission was obliged to revise the delegated act accordingly. This Delegated Act is supported by robust scientific analysis and latest available data and is legally required by the legislative framework agreed by the co-legislators.

Updating the scientific data to determine which feedstocks are classified as high risk is also needed for the EU to comply with the findings in two WTO dispute settlement cases, and the WTO. Should the Delegated Act be blocked, then the EU risks being subject to substantial sanctions, which could target our agricultural exporters.

It is important to underline that the categorisation of soy beans as high-ILUC risk feedstock does not represent a ban. Member States are still free to promote and support biofuels, including from soy beans, as they consider most appropriate. Only the amount of fuels that is counted towards the targets in the Renewable Energy Directive is gradually reduced until 2030.

I would also like to stress that only a small share of biodiesel consumed in the EU is produced from soybeans and the vast majority of it is grown in third countries. Therefore, although some operators in the EU may need to adapt, the economic impact of classifying soya as high ILUC on EU producers and crushing industry should remain limited because the EU livestock sector continues to rely on soyabean and there are alternative outlets for soya oil, including food, feed and industrial uses. Strong global demand and high soyabean oil prices, together with possible lower EU imports and export opportunities, should further help limit negative effects on suppliers and the soya industry.

Independently from that, work is currently ongoing on ways to review the low ILUC-risk certification procedure, so that producers of soy beans that receive such certification will be exempted from the categorisation of a feedstock as high-ILUC risk, and we will further assess in setting-up the renewable energy framework for the decade ahead how we can further support domestic biofuel production as well as the farming sector.

2026-07-08ConsentA10-0151/2026EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement

Discussion transcript

EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

The next vote is on the EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement (see minutes, item 10.8).

Paolo BORCHIA

Mr President, honourable colleagues, we are proceeding with a vote that represents a technical alignment for Morocco's participation in PRIMA, the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area, with a focus on water, agriculture, and food security.

This vote will guarantee its continuity until 2031, with no budgetary implications.

I also take this opportunity to thank my colleagues on the ITRE Committee, who voted for the measure in committee almost unanimously.

That being said, however, I would like to broaden the reflection to the topic of agriculture, given that we cannot look at an agreement with Morocco without extending our vision to a broader framework of relations, particularly on the agricultural front.

In the last two months of 2025 alone, Morocco covered over 70% of extra-EU imports regarding tomatoes, a flow that has quadrupled over the last twenty years.

Therefore, this report would also like to open a reflection on the issue that the Commission should monitor the implementation of these types of agreements, even those referring to research and innovation, with particular attention to agricultural imports, so that the principles of reciprocity and fair competition are respected.

We propose an amendment in the following wording (I will read it right now): "The European Parliament demands memory for the 100,000 brutally murdered Poles and Jews in the Volhynian slaughter; firmly rejects the cult of bandits from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and Stepan Bandera, who are responsible for genocide and cooperation with Hitler; calls on the Ukrainian authorities to immediately cease their state commemoration and glorification; cultivating the memory of genocide perpetrators is contrary to morality and European values; therefore, we call on the Ukrainian authorities to unequivocally reject the glorification of persons responsible for genocide; emphasizes that Banderite ideology is a mirror image of Nazi ideology and - like Nazism - Banderism must be recognized as a banned ideology in the European Union."

Gilles PENNELLE

Mr President, the prospect of Ukraine's accession to the European Union would constitute a major threat to our nations' agriculture. Our farmers have already been suffering the consequences since 2022. The liberalization of Ukrainian agricultural imports, which only the Patriots group fought against from the very start, has led to the massive influx of sugar, cereals, and poultry onto the European market, to the detriment of our producers' incomes.

Yet the Commission wants to go further. In its new vegetable protein strategy presented yesterday, it confirms its abandonment of the ambition to see European agriculture satisfy our needs for vegetable protein, in order to worsen imports from Ukraine.

I therefore propose the following amendment to create a new paragraph 32: "stresses that the Commission, in its latest protein strategy, proposes to rely on Ukraine's agricultural production capacity to remedy the shortage of vegetable protein in the Union, instead of favoring the development of European production".

Petras AUŠTREVIČIUS

Mr President, colleagues, let me move the following oral amendment:

'Welcomes the valuable talks between the Ministers for Foreign Affairs of Poland and Ukraine, held in Warsaw on 3 July, which demonstrated the goodwill of both sides to resolve the existing tensions before they develop into a crisis; calls for an open and constructive dialogue between the Polish and Ukrainian authorities, historians and civil societies in order to restore the indispensable trust between the two countries.'

Sergey LAGODINSKY

Mr President, I would like to draw your attention to some of the chants that were uttered here from that side of the Chamber, when somebody dared to stand in opposition to one of the oral amendments. People – colleagues – were called Nazis just because they dared to have a different position on something, which is very sensitive, but we do not share the style of calling each other Nazis. Some of the real Nazis...

(Protests)

Some of the real Nazis who are present in this Chamber are never called as such during the sessions here. I have never heard anyone call each other that. I would like to ask you to identify and to sanction those who are attacking their colleagues just for their opinion here, who dare to oppose that amendment.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

Colleague, we take note of your remarks. We will check the recording. It's very important to respect the Rules of this House.

Colleague, on the same item? If we open the same item, it will be too much.

Raphaël GLUCKSMANN

Mr President, on the same subject, but not at the time of the same vote, the colleague who sits at seat number 286, I believe, or 288, made an obscene gesture - made an obscene gesture! - at the time of the vote. That gesture was directed towards this part of the assembly. And that is deeply unbearable! You have the right to be Vladimir Putin's relays in this chamber, but do not behave like Russian fascists!

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

Colleagues, please all respect this House and respect ourselves.

We take note of all the remarks. We will give the floor for one more intervention.

Petr BYSTRON

Mr President! Above all, thank you very much to the colleague from Germany who speaks out against colleagues being called Nazis here, because Mr Brandstätter, your kindred spirit, called me, a Czech refugee, “the friendly face of National Socialism” yesterday. I strongly reject that, and I think that should be penalised.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

Colleagues, we take note of all the remarks, and I want to assure you that in the Bureau of this House, the issue of respecting the Rules of the House has been discussed.

2026-07-07Second readingC10-0178/2026Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse

Discussion transcript

Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

The first vote is on the request by the EPP Group for an urgent decision on the temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse (see minutes, item 7.1).

I give the floor first to Tomas Tobé to speak in favour of the urgent decision.

Tomas TOBÉ

Madam President, dear colleagues, today's vote is not about party politics. Today's vote is not about majority tactics or strategy. Today's vote is not about shared control. It is not even about procedures. It is much more important than that. Today's vote is about deciding if we want to protect our children, or if we want to protect sexual predators.

Madam President, in March, we collectively failed to protect children. But in April, this House, together, clearly urged the Commission to come up with measures to close the legal gap that we currently have. The Commission has acted, and 26 out of 27 Member States have agreed.

Colleagues, we have a unique chance right now to send a clear signal – we care. We care about our children, and we will protect them because behind every child that is exposed on sexual abuse materials online is a victim that is never heard, and an offender that is never brought to justice. Without the interim regulation, 99 % of child abuse material goes undetected. This is unacceptable. We cannot go to summer recess knowing that our children are not protected.

So I say to all you colleagues, please take responsibility today. Vote today in favour of the urgent resolution to protect children on Thursday. And then we continue our work together on the permanent regulation. Vote to protect children.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

I give the floor now to Mary Khan to speak against.

Mary KHAN

Madam President! Summer, sun, mass surveillance. That is how some EU elites imagine the start of the summer holidays. Shortly before the break, a surveillance structure is supposed to be pushed through quickly. And that, even though Parliament has already rejected chat control. Now the exact same proposal is simply being warmed up again.

In this august House of democracy, votes apparently continue to be held until the result fits. You all know very well that there is no majority for permanent chat control. That is why they are now trying, together with the Council, to revive the whole thing through the back door; that is why, as so often, they are once again choosing the salami-slicing tactic.

Translated, this means: private messages are to be made technically searchable, images, videos and even texts automatically checked. The fact that an attempt is being made today to push the whole thing through via an urgency motion clearly shows the spirit of this project.

Since 2021, Ursula von der Leyen has been trying to gain access to our private messages. She herself cannot disclose her SMS: everyone knows what was going on on our continent in 2021 during the time of the corona measures.

And of course – this argument does not hold water, I am a mother myself – of course we all want to protect children. But real child protection does not begin with putting every citizen under general suspicion. Real child protection begins where perpetrators genuinely become dangerous: with harsh sentences instead of probation; open perpetrator registries are needed; with better law enforcement and the dismantling of grooming gangs. Anyone who handles child molesters with kid gloves but wants to put millions of citizens under general suspicion is deliberately setting the wrong priorities.

And to every citizen: every citizen can see today, and should also do so, which MEP voted today to make their private messages searchable in the future. Look closely! Remember the names! Every MEP who votes for this urgency motion is also voting for mass surveillance.

Discussion transcript

Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

The next vote is on the financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025 (see minutes, item 7.13).

Jorge BUXADÉ VILLALBA

Madam President, Ms Nadia Calviño, former minister of Sánchez and now at the head of the European Investment Bank, announced on social media the allocation of 365 million EUR for roads and railways in Morocco.

Therefore, we believe it is important to include the following amendment: Regrets the allocation by the European Investment Bank of 365 million EUR to reinforce the resilience and security of Morocco's road and rail networks, as announced by the Bank's President, Nadia Calviño, on 30 June 2026.

Recalls that these financial resources should be allocated as a priority to improving transport infrastructure within the Union, especially in light of the serious railway accidents that have occurred in recent years, which have highlighted deficiencies in the maintenance and modernisation of transport infrastructure in several Member States.

Considers that such funding does not comply with the Bank's primary mission, established in Article 309 of the Treaty on the Functioning, consisting in contributing to the balanced and steady development of the internal market in the interest of the Union.

2026-07-07A10-0169/2026A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector

Discussion transcript

A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

The next vote is on a coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector (see minutes, item 7.16).

Matthias ECKE

Madam President, colleagues, we cannot carry on like this. This is not sustainable. Our financial sector taxation system needs reform. Europe needs more investment for our digital and green transitions to strengthen our security and to foster investment. We need a deeper integrated financial market, but our taxation system has not kept up with that challenge. The VAT exemption on financial services dates back to 1977. This is nearly 50 years and it was designed for an entirely different financial system. Today, it creates distortions and it undermines our single market.

There is no simple solution for that. This is why this report is proposing no specific recipe, but it calls on the Commission to thoroughly investigate the matter and to propose a coherent framework. And to be honest, colleagues, I expect ambition. I expect the Commission to also assess the role that financial transaction tax and windfall taxes can play in such a framework. We should also take a hard look on whether national tax regimes for the financial sector contribute to harmful tax competition in the European Union and sustain tax havens.

Colleagues, the shortcomings of the current system have led to more than 90 different national sectoral taxations – more than 90 – across the Union. So, this patchwork creates unnecessary complexity and bureaucracy. It distorts the single market and it ultimately weakens European competitiveness. After almost 50 years, it's time for a change. It's time to modernise. I want you to be part of that modernisation. I am asking for your support.

2026-07-07A10-0173/2026A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning

Discussion transcript

A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

The next vote is on a new strategy for media literacy and digital learning (see minutes, item 7.17).

Marcos ROS SEMPERE

Madam President, for a long time we viewed the expansion of the internet and social networks with optimism. We thought that information would circulate freely and that public conversation would be more open. However, the digital space that completely permeates us has changed radically, and that optimism has become clouded. The concentration of power in few hands, opacity, and a business model based on permanent addiction have profoundly transformed that ecosystem. Disinformation circulates easily, manipulated content multiplies, and artificial intelligence has accelerated and multiplied this effect.

Understanding how this new world works must be a democratic priority today. Decades ago, we understood that full citizenship did not exist without knowing how to read and write. Today, something similar happens to us: in the digital era, no one can fully exercise their rights if they do not distinguish reality from disinformation, if they do not recognize manipulation generated by artificial intelligence, or if they do not understand how algorithms work. And if our citizenry does not have those tools, our democracies are not prepared for this new digital era.

Ladies and gentlemen, no member state can face this challenge alone. That is why today we are voting to implement a new media literacy and digital learning strategy for all of Europe. A strategy that recognizes these competencies as basic and essential for all citizens, at any age and throughout their lives, especially for boys, girls, and adolescents. It will serve for their protection against harassment, inappropriate content, and addictive design, as well as for our elderly and society as a whole, because no one can be free in a digital environment they do not understand.

Media and digital literacy is a democratic necessity, and today we are sending a clear message. Thank you for your vote.

2026-07-07A10-0187/2026Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum

Discussion transcript

Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

The next vote is on the implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum (see minutes, item 7.18).

Lukas MANDL

Madam President, colleagues, the United Nations are more needed now than in decades before. The world needs the United Nations. At the same time, the United Nations need a reform. There is an urgent need for a reform.

I thank the co-negotiators here in the European Parliament, especially Pierfrancesco Maran, for tough negotiations, but constructive negotiations to receive a good result for next week's high-level political forum at the UN headquarters in New York to represent the European stance for a rule-based international order.

And I also want to say to some who criticised the Sustainable Development Goals: we have to see them holistically. We have to see them balanced and we have to follow them in a balanced approach. Also, economic growth is part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Also education. Also innovation that drives the economy is part of the SDGs. So if we follow the SDGs in an unideological way and follow them in a balanced way in our operative work, we contribute to a positive outcome.

Pierfrancesco MARAN

Madam President, dear colleagues, sustainability, competitiveness and social justice must go hand in hand. More than a decade ago, the world came together to adopt the 2030 agenda. Since then, millions have escaped poverty and gained access to education, clean water and electricity. Yet today, progress is slowing as conflict and climate change put those achievements at risk.

Next week, at the United Nations High‑Level Political Forum, Parliament will contribute to accelerating the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals. Leadership means responsibility. Europe must lead by example by advancing climate neutrality, affordable clean energy and stronger international partnership.
